questions.stem: How will you differentiate a mediastinal mass being a thymoma or acute lymphoblastic leukemia?
questions.solutionHtml:
Cytokeratin

A mediastinal mass has a differential of thymoma and T-cell ALL.

T-cell ALL will have the markers TDT (lymphoblast), CD1a and CD3.

Thymoma has 2 components- epithelial and lymphoid components—so is positive for EMA, cytokeratin 7 and 20, CD57 CD5, bcl-2, calretinin, vimentin, CD3, CD1a, CD20, CD99.

To differentiate between a mediastinal mass being a thymoma or acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), the following immunohistochemical markers can be helpful: 

  1. Cytokeratin: Thymomas typically express cytokeratin, which is a marker for epithelial cells. Positive staining for cytokeratin suggests an epithelial origin, supporting a diagnosis of thymoma.
  2. CD1a: CD1a is a marker for immature T-cells. It is typically positive in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) but negative in thymomas.
  3. CD3: CD3 is a marker for mature T-cells. It is usually positive in T-ALL, including both T-cell and mature T-cell subtypes. In contrast, thymomas are typically negative for CD3.
  1. TdT (Terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase): TdT is an enzyme expressed in immature lymphoid cells, and its expression is characteristic of ALL. Thymomas are usually negative for TdT.

By evaluating the expression of these markers, a pathologist can assess the cell lineage and differentiation status of the cells within the mediastinal mass, helping to differentiate between thymoma and ALL. However, it's important to note that these markers should be interpreted in conjunction with clinical findings, imaging studies, and other diagnostic tests for a comprehensive diagnosis.



Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th Edition, Page No. 593

questions.stem: Naive T cells get activated by:
questions.solutionHtml:
Dendritic cells

Antigen presenting cells are cells that present Antigen to T cells 

  • Antigen-presenting cells (APCs) capture microbes and other antigens, transport them to secondary lymphoid organs, and display them for recognition by lymphocytes.
  • The most efficient APCs are dendritic cells (DCs), which are present in epithelia and most other tissues.
  • Integrins are adhesion molecules that promote the attachment of T-cells to APCs.
  • They express high levels of MHC and other molecules needed for presenting antigens to and activating T cells.


Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th Edition, Page No. 195, 196, 198-201

questions.stemHtml: A patient presented with intermittent fever, no weight loss, no anorexia, but with a retroperitoneal mass. Peripheral smear findings were normal. Gross and microscopy of the mass is given. What is the diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Castleman disease

Castleman disease has been divided into a solitary and a multicentric form. The solitary form presents as a mass located most commonly in the mediastinum, neck, lung, axilla, mesentery, broad ligament, and retroperitoneum. Grossly, it is round, well circumscribed, with a solid gray cut surface and measures >15 cm in diameter. The follicles show marked vascular proliferation and hyalinization of their abnormal or atrophic germinal centers, surrounded by concentrically arranged small lymphocytes imparting an “onion-skin” pattern. Remember angiolymphoid hyperplasia shows thick-walled blood vessels with prominent endothelial cells and inflammatory eosinophilia infiltrates.



https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK576394/#:~:text=Castleman%20disease%2

questions.stem: A patient comes with severe bleeding. PRBCs and 4 units of platelet concentrates have been collected from the blood bank. With only one IV access what will you do?

options.label: A
options.text: Transfuse PRBC first and store platelets at room temperature

options.label: B
options.text: Transfuse PRBC first and store platelets at 2–6°C

options.label: C
options.text: Transfuse platelets first and store PRBC at 2–6°C

options.label: D
options.text: Transfuse platelets first and store PRBC at room temperature

questions.answerText: Transfuse platelets first and store PRBC at room temperature
questions.solutionHtml:
Transfuse platelets first and store PRBC at room temperature
  • The transfusion time of the PRBC (Packed Red Blood Cells) is 100–150 mL/hour and that of platelets and plasma is 150–300 mL/hour.
  • So while the platelets are transfused, the RBC can be stored at room temperature. If we do the other way round, the transfusion of platelets will need to wait for 4 hours which will not only reduce the clinical utility (remember, the patient is bleeding), but will also decrease the increase in platelet count in the recipient (Dilutional thrombocytopenia).
  • Also, the PRBC needs to be transfused within 4 hours while platelets need to be transfused as soon as possible. Clinically, this answer makes more sense than the other options.


Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th Edition, Page No. 671, 672, Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 20th Edition, Page No. 813, 814

questions.stem: Integrin connects actin to which macromolecule in ECM?
questions.solutionHtml:
Fibronectin

Fibronectin > Laminin 

Integrins are bound to fibronectin or other ECM proteins adsorbed to the substrate or incorporated into the insoluble matrix, and connect to the actin through linker proteins such as talin and vinculin.



Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th Edition, Page No. 24

questions.stem: A patient present with steatorrhea and abnormal Schilling test. D-xylose test is normal and nor
questions.solutionHtml:
Ileal disease
  • The given clinical scenario with steatorrhea (Presence of excess fat in stool), abnormal schilling test suggests malabsorption of B12.
  • The normal D-xylose test result indicates that the patient's small intestine is capable of absorbing monosaccharides, which rules out significant malabsorption in the proximal small bowel.
  • Hence, among the following options the correct option is Ileal disease.


Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th Edition, Chapter 15

questions.stem: A trauma patient presents at the emergency department. There is no time for cross-matching. FFP of which blood group can be transfused safely?
questions.solutionHtml:
AB Rh, D Negative
  1. Universal blood donor = O Negative
  2. Universal acceptor = AB Positive
  3. Universal FFP donor = AB Positive
  4. Universal FFP acceptor = O Negative


Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th Edition, Page No. 671, 672, Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 20th Edition, Page No. 813, 814

questions.stem: Antibody dependent killing is mediated by:
questions.solutionHtml:
NK cells, neutrophils, and macrophages
  • Antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC) is the killing of an antibody-coated target cell by a cytotoxic effector cell through a non phagocytic process, characterized by the release of content of cytotoxic granules or by expression of cell death-inducing.
  • ADCC is triggered through the interaction of target-bound antibodies (IgG, IgE) with certain Fc receptors and glycoproteins present on the effector cell surface that bind the Fc region of lg. Effector cells that mediate ADCC include NK cells, monocytes, macrophages, neutrophils, eosinophils, and dendritic cells.
  • The function of NK cells is to recognize and destroy severely stressed or abnormal cells, such as virus-infected cells and tumor cells.


Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th Edition, Page No. 192, 209

questions.stemHtml: Immunofluorescence staining pattern from the kidney biopsy of a 35-year-old patient presenting with proteinuria is shown below. What is the most probable cause?
questions.solutionHtml:
Lupus nephritis
  • The given immunofluorescence staining of the kidney biopsy shows positive staining for fibrinogen, IgG, IgA, IgM, C1q, C3, κ lights chains and λ light chains. This is the typical “full-house” pattern with intense (+++) granular staining for IgA, IgG, IgM, kappa and lambda and C1 and C3 in a diffuse mesangiocapillary pattern can be seen which is suggestive of SLE.
  • A variety of kidney lesions can be caused by SLE. In a kidney biopsy specimen, if all five major immunofluorescent stains (IgA, IgG, IgM, C3, and C1Q) are positive, then it is considered as full-house immunofluorescence. Full-house immunofluorescence and endothelial tubuloreticular inclusions are known as characteristic features of lupus nephritis.


Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th Edition, Page No. 221-229. Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 20th Edition, Page No. 2515-2526
